patterns.text: Pattern TP1-00069 (single place). Place: the U.S. state of Arizona (NCA5 region: Southwest). Quantity: days hot and humid enough to be dangerous. Season: summer. Horizon: by mid-century, compared with the modeled historical baseline. Scenario: under a high-emissions future. Statistic: change of the mean (future minus modeled historical baseline). Direction: increase. Value: +10.3 days. Mean: 13.9 days in the modeled historical baseline, 24.2 days at mid-century. Range of the change per grid cell: 0.0 to 27.1 days. Robustness: 1976 of 2007 grid cells change in the same direction as the mean (majority_same_direction). Comparison with other U.S. states: a change similar to most states (by signed value, among 49 U.S. states for this quantity, season, horizon, scenario and statistic; a relative descriptor among states, not an absolute threshold).

groups.label: Large-scale warming and land–atmosphere feedbacks drive increases in extreme heat

members.statement: Citing Schoof et al. (2019), the paper reports that large-scale warming, rather than changes in regional circulation, is the primary driver of future changes in extreme heat.
members.passage: However, recent work examining changes in the frequency of different types of extreme heat days (considering both temperature and humidity) in CMIP5 projections after using a multivariate quantile mapping approach similar to the MACA methodology finds that large-scale warming, rather than changes in regional circulation, is the primary driver of future changes in extreme heat (Schoof et al 2019).

members.statement: Land-atmosphere feedbacks are a stronger factor for heat wave maintenance at southern latitudes, and misrepresentation of these feedbacks in models leads to poor forecast skill in the Southwest United States.
members.passage: Land-atmosphere feedbacks appear to be a stronger factor for heat wave maintenance at southern latitudes, but the NCEP model seems to misrepresent those feedbacks, particularly over the Southwest United States, leading to poor skill in that region.

members.statement: Air mass stagnation events, which boost ozone production, are expected to become more frequent as weather conditions that favor heat waves increase.
members.passage: Air mass stagnation events, which increase O3 production and will increase in frequency as weather conditions favorable to heat waves increase (CCSP 2008), are another important indicator.

groups.label: global warming increases heatwave frequency and intensity

members.statement: Projected climate warming is expected to increase the frequency, intensity, and duration of heatwaves, thereby elevating heat‑stress risk.
members.passage: As global warming continues, the frequency, intensity and duration of heatwaves are likely to increase.

members.statement: Climate change is causing heat waves to occur more often and with greater intensity.
members.passage: With climate change, heat waves have become more frequent and intense.

members.statement: Anthropogenic global warming is expected to increase both the mean annual temperature and the frequency of heat events.
members.passage: The occurrence of heat events is expected to increase due to the worsening effects of anthropogenic global warming [60]. This will be seen in both higher mean annual temperatures and in the frequency of heat shocks [37].

members.statement: Global warming is expected to increase the frequency of extreme heat events, raising heat exposure for agricultural workers.
members.passage: Climate change has resulted in a significant rise in the global mean temperature and it is predicted to get worse [23]. This means more extreme heat events and heat exposure for people working in agriculture in the hot climates.

groups.label: urban heat island intensifies due to nighttime conditions and reduced moisture

members.statement: The urban heat island effect is most pronounced at night and under high‑pressure, calm, clear‑sky conditions.
members.passage: Further, the UHI is most noticeable at night and under synoptic high pressure systems with calm conditions and clear skies [24,[26][27][28], and the UHI has been measured in cities spanning many varying climate regimes and sizes [29][30][31][32].

members.statement: During heat‑wave events, CUHI intensifies markedly, especially at night, because urban areas experience lower moisture and reduced wind speed.
members.passage: In general, simulated CUHI values during a heat wave have intensified extensively relative to pre-heat wave conditions, mostly due to the lower moisture and reduced wind speed in urban areas during the heat wave.

members.statement: During daytime, evapotranspiration from vegetation is the primary cooling mechanism, but it often cannot fully offset heat gains from advection and sensible heat from impervious surfaces.
members.passage: During the daytime, evapotranspiration is the main cooling mechanism, however its impact on the surface energy budget may not be enough to compensate and counterbalance heat fluxes due to advection and sensible heat released by the impervious surfaces.

members.statement: In extreme heat or drought conditions, trees may close their stomata, reducing evapotranspiration and potentially adding sensible heat, thereby diminishing their cooling effect.
members.passage: During excessive temperature and drought conditions, trees may close their stomata while the surface temperature of leaves increases, contributing more sensible heat to the atmosphere and increasing the ambient temperature [150,151].

members.statement: The cooling benefit of urban greenery is generally larger at night than during the day because trees reduce stored daytime heat and emit less sensible heat at night.
members.passage: During the night, the maximum ambient temperature decrease corresponding to a GI rise of 80% may not exceed 2.3 • C, while the temperature drop for a GI increase by 20% is close to 0.5 • C.

groups.label: humidity magnifies heat stress and its effect grows with temperature

members.statement: The magnifying effect of relative humidity on heat stress grows with increasing temperature, so that even unchanged or lower humidity can cause greater discomfort at higher temperatures.
members.passage: at similar or lower humidity, the magnifying power of humidity increases with increasing T, i.e. similar or lower relative humidity levels will still cause greater human discomfort at higher temperatures.

guardrails: A modeled historical baseline is model output for a past period, not an observation.
A Fire Weather Index is a meteorological fire-danger index; it is never fire occurrence, ignition, burned area or damage.
A high-emissions future is one plausible future, not a forecast and not the only plausible future.
Hazard is not exposure, and exposure is not risk.
Research on an asset class describes what such conditions can do to that kind of asset; it is not a forecast for a particular asset at the place.
Impact statements are general unless a group is marked place_named for the place.
model_view.rung_name: 8. Hazard impact on infrastructure: State the projected hazard change at a place and what research shows such conditions do to an asset class.
model_view.rung_instruction: Rung 8 (hazard impact on infrastructure). Write the answer in three parts: (1) the hazard change at the place, as projected, in the table-pattern sentence; (2) for the impact groups, '<scope phrase> that <hazard phrase> <impact mechanism> <asset class phrase>', where the hazard phrase is the broader-hazard phrase when a cited impact group has hazard_relation broader_hazard, else the plain quantity; the driver groups as in any item; the general closing clause when no cited group is state- or NCA-specific; (3) never state that an asset, or the asset class, in the place will fail, is at risk, is vulnerable or will be damaged. Only when citing a group listed in place_named_impact_group_ids may the answer write 'For <asset class phrase> in <Place>, this implies more exposure to <impact outcome>'.
